name: Lead-Safe Window Replacement Practices for Older LA County Homes

mainEntity.name: What precautions should Los Angeles County homeowners take when replacing windows in homes built before 1978 that may contain lead paint?
mainEntity.text: What precautions should Los Angeles County homeowners take when replacing windows in homes built before 1978 that may contain lead paint?

acceptedAnswer.text: Homes built before 1978 in Los Angeles County may contain lead-based paint, particularly around windows where friction and chipping are common. Disturbing these surfaces during replacement can release hazardous dust. Homeowners should choose contractors trained in lead-safe work practices, which include setting up containment with plastic sheeting, minimizing dust generation, and using HEPA vacuums for cleanup. Ask whether the crew is certified for lead-safe renovation and how they handle scraping, cutting, and disposal of old sashes and trim. Dry sanding, open-flame burning, or uncontrolled demolition should be avoided because they spread lead dust. Interiors should be protected, and access to work areas limited, especially for children and pregnant occupants. Expect some additional labor and material costs for containment, protective gear, and detailed cleaning. Clarify in the contract who is responsible for final cleaning and whether any post-work dust testing is offered. Planning ahead by removing or covering nearby items, sealing HVAC registers during work, and scheduling at times when vulnerable occupants can be out of the house can further reduce risk while allowing window upgrades to proceed safely.
acceptedAnswer.description: For pre-1978 homes in Los Angeles County, window replacement should follow lead-safe practices: using certified crews, containing dust with plastic sheeting, avoiding unsafe sanding, thorough cleanup, and proper disposal. Homeowners should confirm contractors’ training and discuss any extra costs tied to lead compliance.
